framing_conflicts.claim: Under label (composition) shift, alignment with any proper divergence forces errors, and tighter alignment forces more (Zhao 2019 Thm 4.3; Wu 2019)
framing_conflicts.finding: Zhao 2019 Thm 4.3 (PMLR p7) is stated for binary hypotheses with the JS distance on the representation; "tighter forces more" holds in JS-distance terms only. For any divergence the error is forced only at exact alignment (a distance that is zero only for identical distributions), which is Wu 2019 Prop. 3.1 (PMLR p3), also for binary labels. The outline words it this way.

framing_conflicts.claim: scIB-E compares GAN, HSIC, orthogonality and MI losses in scVI/scANVI
framing_conflicts.finding: scIB-E level 1 has six losses: GAN, HSIC, orthogonal projection, MIM, reverse backpropagation (gradient reversal) and reverse cross-entropy (Genome Biol 26:398, p4); levels 2-3 add label-aware losses in scANVI. The absence of W1, MMD and OT is confirmed (0 occurrences of Wasserstein, MMD, maximum mean, optimal transport, Sinkhorn in the full text). The outline lists all six.

framing_conflicts.claim: In GANs the loss is second-order to tuning and regularisation (Lucic 2018; Kurach 2019)
framing_conflicts.finding: Lucic 2018 (p1) supports: similar scores with enough tuning and restarts; no algorithm consistently beats the non-saturating GAN. Kurach 2019 supports: the non-saturating loss is stable; spectral normalisation consistently helps; the gradient penalty has no clear trend (p5). Neither paper ranks the loss below regularisation in those words, and both are image-GAN studies. The outline states the findings, not "second-order".

framing_conflicts.claim: The JS-vs-W1 premise becomes a tested hypothesis
framing_conflicts.finding: SI-68 (user decision, 2026-10-14) makes the premise check R0 exploratory, with no confirmed or refuted claim. The ledger wins; the outline says the premise is examined, not tested.

framing_conflicts.claim: Defensible gap: no budget-matched JS vs W1 vs MMD/OT comparison on a stock scVI backbone trained on real counts
framing_conflicts.finding: SI-15 fits the scIB files as distributed (the counts layer as scIB fed scVI; no strict-count main run), so "trained on real counts" is dropped. The rest of the gap holds as a search-based absence; re-searched 2026-10-15 (4 OpenAlex queries from 2024 on, 52 works, and 1 web search): no such comparison found.

framing_conflicts.claim: scVI's adversary trains on reparameterised posterior samples, so continuous noise removes the disjoint-support condition (Arjovsky & Bottou 2017 Thm 3.1)
framing_conflicts.finding: True for the stock scvi-tools adversary (arm scvi_adv runs AdversarialTrainingPlan unchanged; z = inference_outputs["z"], scvi-tools 1.4.2 _trainingplans.py:689; Encoder rsample, _base_components.py:304-305). The authored arms use the posterior mean by default (SI-19; scripts/scvi_adversarial_plan.py:359), which adds no noise; the R2 switch to samples is pending. The manifest of record lists adv_input = mean for the 40 X1 scvi_adv rows, a value that arm does not read.

framing_conflicts.claim: The theory covers the saturating loss; the bounded fool loss is not covered automatically
framing_conflicts.finding: Confirmed and sharpened: for two batches the fool loss (scripts/scvi_adversarial_plan.py:292-298) is the label-flipped non-saturating loss; Arjovsky & Bottou Thms 2.4-2.6 assume a fixed data distribution and a moving generator, whereas every batch latent moves here.

framing_conflicts.claim: IMAAE employs a Wasserstein-based adversarial autoencoder to tackle scenarios where cell types are disjoint across batches
framing_conflicts.finding: The IMAAE text never uses "Wasserstein" or "WGAN" (0 occurrences, PMC full text); its losses have WGAN-GP form (gradient penalty on interpolates, generator loss -E[D]); it matches the latent to N(0,I), uses an anchor batch and known cell labels. Audit C24 flagged the attribution; re-confirmed.

framing_conflicts.claim: Batch effects arise from the sequencing technology utilized (Tung 2017)
framing_conflicts.finding: Tung 2017 studies separately processed technical replicates on one platform (Fluidigm C1), not sequencing technologies; cited in the outline only for replicate-level batch effects.

framing_conflicts.claim: Integration methods can be broadly categorized into statistical, geometric and deep generative models (Luecken 2022)
framing_conflicts.finding: scIB (p1) groups integration outputs as a graph, a joint embedding or a corrected feature matrix; the three-way taxonomy is the authors' own organisation and is kept without citing scIB for it.

framing_conflicts.finding: Not checked (Stegle 2015 not retrieved); dropped. AD-AE (Dincer 2020, abstract) names age as an uninteresting biological confounder and is cited instead.
